title: Rule, AI, or human: who should do the task?

description: Ten real business tasks. Decide whether each needs rule-based automation, an AI step, or a person, and learn the reasoning behind every answer.
lead: Ten everyday business tasks. For each one, decide whether a simple rule-based automation, an AI step, or a person should handle it. It is the most useful skill in planning automation.

intro.title: Who should do the work?
intro.text: The best automation plans give each task to the right worker: fixed rules for predictable steps, AI for language and judgment within limits, and people for decisions that need authority, empathy, or accountability.
bullets: A quick way to sharpen your automation instincts

questions.q: Send a reminder text 24 hours before every appointment.
questions.why: The timing and the message are fixed. A simple scheduled workflow does this perfectly every time, at almost no cost.

questions.q: Read incoming emails and decide whether each is a sales inquiry, a support request, or an invoice.
questions.why: Emails are free text and vary widely, so keyword rules miss a lot. An AI classification step handles the variety, and unclear cases can be routed to a person.

questions.q: Decide whether to offer a discount to an upset long-time customer.
questions.why: This needs judgment, context, and authority. Automation can pull up the customer's history and flag the situation, but a person should make the call.
link: Guide: how to automate customer support

questions.q: Copy every new paid order from your online store into your accounting software.
questions.why: The data is already structured and the mapping never changes. An integration or simple workflow moves it reliably with no interpretation needed.
link: Guide: how to automate data entry

questions.q: Pull the invoice number, date, vendor, and total from PDF invoices sent by dozens of different suppliers.
questions.why: Every supplier's layout is different, so fixed templates break. AI document extraction copes with the variety, with a person reviewing anything the model is unsure about.
link: Guide: how to automate invoice processing

questions.q: Draft a reply to a detailed customer question using your help articles.
questions.why: Drafting from approved content is a strong AI use case. Keep a person approving replies until you trust the quality, especially for anything involving money or commitments.

questions.q: Negotiate contract terms with a new enterprise client.
questions.why: Negotiation involves relationships, strategy, and binding commitments. AI can help prepare, for example by summarizing the contract, but a person should lead.

questions.q: When a deal is marked won in the CRM, create the project, send the welcome email, and notify the team.
questions.why: A clear trigger followed by the same steps every time is the textbook rule-based workflow. It removes a handoff that often gets delayed.

questions.q: Turn a 40-minute sales call recording into notes and next steps for the CRM.
questions.why: Transcription plus AI summarization handles this well. The workflow can then post the summary to the CRM, with the salesperson skimming it for accuracy.
link: Guide: what is an AI agent?

questions.q: Tell an employee they did not get the promotion they applied for.
questions.why: Sensitive conversations need empathy and accountability. Automation has no place in delivering this message, though it can help schedule the conversation.

bands.title: Keep practicing
bands.text: A useful rule of thumb: if you could write the steps as if-this-then-that, use a rule. If a step involves reading or writing language, consider AI. If it needs authority or empathy, keep a person.

bands.title: Good instincts
bands.text: You can tell predictable work from judgment calls. Next, learn how AI steps fit inside rule-based workflows, with people approving the risky parts.

bands.title: Expert sorter
bands.text: You think like an automation designer. Put that to work on your own task list and find the first workflow to build.

explainer:
A simple way to decide

  • Rule-based automation for predictable steps with structured data: reminders, notifications, moving records between apps, creating tasks.
  • An AI step where the input is language or varies too much for rules: sorting messages, extracting data from documents, summarizing, drafting.
  • A person for decisions that need authority, empathy, negotiation, or accountability, and for reviewing AI output where mistakes are costly.

Most real workflows mix all three. A support workflow might use a rule to log every ticket, AI to sort and draft replies, and a person to approve refunds. The guide to AI vs. automation explains how to combine them.
faq: When should I use AI instead of regular automation?

Use AI when a step requires understanding or producing language, or when inputs vary too much for fixed rules, such as free-text emails or documents in many layouts. Use regular automation for everything predictable; it is cheaper, faster, and easier to audit.
Which tasks should never be automated?

Decisions with legal, financial, or personal consequences that need accountability, such as hiring decisions, sensitive HR conversations, and binding commitments, should stay with people. Automation can still gather information and schedule the work around them.
What does human in the loop mean?
It means the workflow pauses for a person to review or approve a step before it continues, such as approving an AI-drafted email before it is sent.
